rationale: Elihu challenges Job's claim to righteousness before the Lord; his introduction explicitly identifies that same claim as the reason for his anger. The comparison identifies Elihu's objection without endorsing it.

Elihu voices a question about what one will do if one sins. Job earlier asked what he could do to God if he sinned; the conditional sin-and-action question corresponds, although Elihu's version does not repeat the explicit object to Thee.
Elihu promises an answer to Job and the three friends. His introduction describes anger at those friends because they could not answer Job, explaining why he addresses both sides.
Elihu directs attention to the heavens and clouds high above Job; Zophar had invoked heaven's height and the depths to question human understanding of the Almighty's works.
Elihu asks what repeated sin can accomplish against God; Job had asked what he could do to God if he sinned. The matching question belongs to different speakers and arguments.
Elihu asks what a righteous person can give God; Eliphaz had asked what benefit blameless conduct brings the Lord. Both speakers question whether human righteousness supplies God with a benefit.
Elihu asks what God receives from a righteous person's hand. Paul's question asks who first gave to God so that repayment would be owed, similarly rejecting the idea of making God one's debtor.

Elihu describes oppressed people crying under others' power. Israel's laboring people likewise cry in Exodus, where God hears them; that response must be distinguished from Elihu's subsequent explanation of unanswered cries.
Elihu names the Maker who appoints night watches. The psalm assigns both day and night to God and names Him as fashioner of light and sun, linking nighttime order with the Creator.

Elihu distinguishes humanity from four-footed animals and birds. Genesis makes that distinction explicit through humanity's creation in God's image and its authority over birds and cattle; Job does not itself repeat the image language.

Elihu attributes an unheard cry to evil people's insolence. Personified Wisdom likewise refuses the calls of those who rejected her counsel; neither passage establishes that every afflicted person is guilty.

Elihu says the Lord does not wish to see improper things, continuing with His observation of wrongdoers. Zophar says God sees improper things and does not overlook them; the formulations differ while addressing God's regard for wrongdoing.

Elihu challenges Job to enter judgment before God. Job's earlier speech had anticipated stating his case, hearing God's answer and receiving a conclusion from Him, supplying the dispute's judicial context.

Elihu's charge that Job multiplies ignorant words repeats his preceding accusation that Job spoke without understanding or knowledge. These are Elihu's judgments within the debate, not a replacement for God's final assessment.

Elihu requests more time because speech remains within him. Earlier he described himself as full of words, like a wineskin of fermenting wine or a smith's burst bellows, and needing to speak for relief.

Elihu promises true rather than unjust words and challenges Job's understanding. His earlier declaration of a heart pure in words likewise presents his own speech as trustworthy; the link records his self-description.

Elihu's assurance that the Lord will not reject the innocent closely repeats Bildad's declaration. These are statements by Elihu and Bildad respectively; neither by itself proves a particular sufferer's guilt.
Elihu says God gives judgment to the poor; the psalm expressly trusts the Lord to act for the poor person's judgment and the needy people's cause, followed by the righteous person's thanksgiving.

Elihu describes righteous people seated with kings and raised high. Hannah's song describes God lifting the poor to sit with rulers and inherit a throne of glory, sharing the image of God-given elevation.

Elihu describes people held in handcuffs and cords of poverty. The psalm likewise depicts sufferers fettered in poverty and iron, then explains their humiliation; the comparison concerns the bondage image, not Job's proven culpability.

Elihu says God discloses the works and transgressions of the bound sufferers. The psalm explains its prisoners' distress through rejected divine counsel before their appeal to God; both interpret this particular bondage as disciplinary.

Elihu connects God's hearing of the righteous with turning from injustice. Ezekiel explicitly describes a lawless person turning from wrongdoing and practicing righteousness; the shared movement is repentance, while the subjects are described differently.

Elihu says listening and serving lead to good days and splendid years. Deuteronomy promises blessings upon Israel's obedience; this compares the stated obedience-blessing pattern without assigning Israel's covenant conditions directly to Job.

Elihu connects the ungodly person's ruin with refusing to know the Lord and disobeying admonition. Hosea similarly links rejection of knowledge and forgotten divine law with God's rejection of priestly service.

Elihu's hypocrites do not cry out while bound. Hosea distinguishes howling on beds from hearts genuinely crying to God and places this amid discipline, a specific parallel to an insincere response to affliction.

Elihu wishes death and an angel-inflicted wound upon the hypocrites he describes. Acts narrates an angel striking Herod before his death; it supplies a distinct instance of angelic judgment without identifying Herod with Elihu's subjects.

Elihu condemns affliction of weak people and announces judgment for the meek. The psalm commands judges to vindicate and deliver the lowly and needy from a sinner's hand, making protection of the powerless concrete.

Elihu insists judgment will not be lacking to the righteous. The psalm anticipates righteousness returning to judgment and the upright attaching themselves to it, joining justice and righteous people without specifying Job's case.

Elihu condemns gifts accepted for injustices. Exodus forbids justifying the ungodly for gifts and accepting gifts that blind discernment and corrupt righteous words, specifying the judicial corruption in view.

Elihu warns against turning away from the powerless person's plea. The proverb condemns blocking one's ears against the weak and says the refuser's own call will go unheard, sharing the concrete act of refusing an appeal.
Elihu asks who is a ruler like the Strong One. The sea song asks who among the gods is like the Lord, whose wonders establish His incomparable power in a particular deliverance.

Elihu challenges the accusation that God has acted unjustly. Moses' song calls God's works true, His ways judgments, and the Lord free of unrighteousness, stating the conviction underlying that challenge.
Elihu calls God's years boundless. The psalm places God before the formation of mountains and earth and declares His existence from age to age, supplying a specific temporal parallel.
Elihu attributes the numbering of raindrops to God. The wisdom poem had already spoken of God counting rain, repeating the concrete image of precipitation measured by divine knowledge.

Elihu describes clouds shading countless mortals. The psalm recounts God spreading a cloud as shelter for the departing people, a particular historical use of the cloud-covering image rather than an identification of the two scenes.

Elihu says cattle know their appointed resting order. The psalm describes nighttime animal activity and lions returning to their enclosures at sunrise, another portrayal of ordered animal activity and rest.

Elihu asks whether Job's heart is changed away from the body. In the following chapter Elihu describes his own troubled heart as flowing from its place, repeating displaced-heart imagery before the storm description.

Elihu links the cloud's extensions with God's tent. The psalm describes God's surrounding tent through darkness and clouded waters, sharing the particular image of atmospheric covering as a divine tent.

Elihu says God judges peoples and gives food through these weather phenomena. His next chapter describes them as serving discipline or mercy, expanding the contrast between adverse and beneficial divine purposes.

Elihu's troubled heart flowing from its place recalls his preceding question about Job's heart being changed away from the body. The repeated bodily image connects his own response with the reaction he asks of Job.

Elihu opens the storm description by calling attention to the Lord's angry report and mouth. The psalm combines divine anger, dark clouds and the Lord's thunderous voice, a developed parallel to this storm presentation.

Elihu describes the Lord's light across the earth's wings. The psalm describes divine lightning shining upon the inhabited world; the link is the wide reach of light in a storm description, not a claim that Job names lightning here.
Elihu describes thunder as God's forceful voice. The psalm similarly joins the God of glory's thunder over waters with the strength and magnificence of the Lord's voice.

Elihu attributes unknown great wonders to the Strong One. Job himself had described God's great, unsearchable and extraordinary works beyond numbering, a shared claim within otherwise differing speeches.
Elihu depicts God commanding snow and rainstorms. The psalm connects His swiftly sent word with snow, ice and melting waters, likewise presenting weather as responsive to divine command.
Elihu describes wild animals entering shelter and resting on their beds. The psalm describes lions gathering into enclosures at sunrise, another concrete picture of wild animals retiring to shelter.
Elihu places the origin of whirlwinds in chambers. The psalm says the Lord brings winds from His treasuries, using a corresponding storehouse image for winds under divine control.
Elihu connects frost with the Strong One's breath and water's direction with His will. The psalm describes divine ice, then God's sent word and wind melting it into flowing waters.

Elihu presents weather as serving discipline or mercy. Deuteronomy gives a specific covenant example: rain and grass accompany obedience, while idolatry brings heaven's closure and failed produce; the settings and audiences remain distinct.

Elihu says God establishes His works by making light out of darkness. Genesis narrates God's command for light, its appearance and its separation from darkness, providing the corresponding creation scene.

Elihu attributes light out of darkness to God. Paul invokes God's command for light from darkness when describing illumination of human hearts in Christ, explicitly applying creation language to spiritual knowledge.

Elihu attributes knowledge of cloud divisions to God. His preceding conditional statement considers understanding a cloud's extensions and God's tent; the passages share the specific subject of cloud formations while using different grammatical forms.
Elihu asks what can be said to God and urges fewer words. Job later asks what answer he can give, covers his mouth and declines to add more, a narrative instance of restrained speech before God.

Elihu describes northern clouds gleaming like gold in connection with divine glory. Ezekiel's vision begins with a northern wind, a great luminous cloud and an electrum-like appearance; this compares imagery without equating Elihu's description with Ezekiel's vision.
Elihu combines incomparable strength with righteous judgment. He had just asked who rules like the Strong One and who could accuse Him of injustice, repeating both elements of the argument.
Elihu says even those wise in heart will fear God. The wisdom poem identifies reverence for God as wisdom and abstaining from evil as knowledge, directly joining the two qualities.
The Lord first addresses Job through a whirlwind and clouds; His renewed reply is again from the cloud. These narrative notices frame the two portions of the divine answer.

God's speech to Job comes through whirlwind and clouds. At Sinai cloud, thunder and other signs accompany God's spoken answer to Moses; both depict divine speech amid atmospheric manifestations without identifying the occasions.

The Lord questions the one concealing counsel and words. Job's final answer repeats that question and then acknowledges wonderful things he did not understand, making the reprise explicit within the dialogue.
The instruction to gird his waist and answer God's questions is repeated in the second divine address. The matching wording marks the renewed challenge rather than a separate human achievement.
The Lord asks where Job was when He founded the earth. The psalm likewise attributes the earth's founding at the beginning to the Lord and calls the heavens His handiwork.

Job is challenged about his absence when earth was founded. Personified Wisdom, by contrast, describes being present with God as He strengthened earth's foundations; this compares the literary witnesses without identifying Job with Wisdom.

The Lord questions Job about earth's measures and measuring cord. Isaiah likewise asks who measured water, heaven, earth and mountains, presenting creation's dimensions as a demonstration of divine capability.

The question about earth's fixed rings and cornerstone uses foundation imagery. The psalm similarly describes the earth as founded upon stability by God, without supplying a literal construction plan for either image.

Stars coming to be and angels praising accompany the earth's foundation scene. The psalm summons angels and stars to praise the Lord because He commanded their creation, joining the same heavenly participants and creative act.

The Lord describes confining the emerging sea with gates. Genesis narrates His gathering of waters into their places and naming the seas; the descriptions use different images for divine ordering of the waters.

The Lord clothes the sea with cloud and mist. The psalm calls the deep a covering like a garment; both employ clothing imagery for cosmic waters, without requiring the same thing to be clothed in each image.

The Lord describes placing boundaries, bars and gates around the sea. Jeremiah attributes the sea's unpassable sand boundary to His enduring command, supplying a close parallel to divinely imposed limits.

relationship: waves unable to cross God's limit
rationale: The Lord tells the sea its waves may advance no farther. The psalm likewise says God set a boundary the waters will not cross or overrun to cover the earth.

relationship: divine order of day and light
rationale: The Lord questions Job about ordering morning brightness and the dawn-bearer's place. The psalm assigns day, night, fashioned light and sun to God, locating this temporal and luminous order in Him.

The dawn is pictured shaking the ungodly from the earth. The royal psalm likewise associates mornings with removing the land's lawless people; this is a poetic judgment parallel with different speakers and actions.
The Lord asks whether Job molded earth and clay into a living, speaking creature. Genesis attributes formation of the human from earth's dust and the gift of life to God.

The Lord's question to Job combines formation from earth with living speech. Sirach likewise describes the Lord creating humanity from earth and granting a tongue and understanding, preserving the connection between material origin and human capacities.
The Lord asks about crushing the arrogant person's arm. The psalm predicts the breaking of sinners' arms while the Lord sustains the righteous, using the same bodily image for defeated power.

Job is questioned about walking the abyss's tracks. The psalm places God's way and paths in the sea while declaring His tracks unknowable, contrasting divine passage through waters with human knowledge of it.

The Lord asks whether death's gates and Hades' gatekeepers fear Job. Hezekiah instead describes approaching Hades' gates as a mortal losing his remaining years; the shared gate image highlights the difference in agency.

The Lord asks whether Job knows the breadth of the realm beneath heaven. Isaiah's question about measuring the whole earth in a handful likewise treats comprehension of its extent as a divine capability.

The question about where light and darkness dwell addresses realities Genesis presents as ordered and distinguished by God. Genesis supplies their creative ordering, not a geographical answer to Job's poetic question.

The Lord's ironic claim that Job was born then and has many years recalls Eliphaz's question whether Job preceded the hills. Both challenge presumed access to primordial wisdom through supposed great age.
The Lord asks about stores of snow and hail. Deuteronomy depicts heaven as God's good treasury opened to provide rain, sharing the treasury image while naming different forms of precipitation.

Hail stored for a day of war has a concrete narrative counterpart when the Lord hurls hailstones against Israel's fleeing enemies. Joshua explicitly distinguishes these deaths from those caused by Israel's swords.

The Lord's questions about frost and the south wind revisit Elihu's description of whirlwinds from chambers, cold from heights and frost from divine breath. The question and earlier assertion retain their different speakers.

relationship: rain and a path for tumult
rationale: The Lord asks who prepared a flow for violent rain and a path for tumult. The wisdom poem had spoken of God counting rain and a path for sounds amid shaking, a close parallel in both weather and path language.

The Lord describes rain upon land where no human lives. Genesis similarly describes ground before there was a man to cultivate it and a spring watering it; the shared contrast concerns divine watering apart from human cultivation.

The Lord describes watering uninhabited ground until green growth sprouts. Isaiah calls the thirsty wilderness to flower and rejoice in God's glory; this compares desert renewal imagery rather than treating Job as a prediction of that oracle.

The Lord asks who fathers rain and dew. Jeremiah's drought prayer asks whether idols or heaven provide rain and answers by appealing to the God who made these things, locating precipitation's origin in Him.

The questions about the birth of ice and heavenly frost parallel the psalm's attribution of snow, ice, cold and their melting to God's action. Neither passage credits humans with control of these conditions.

The Lord asks whether Job understood the Pleiades' bond and opened Orion's enclosure. Job earlier named God as maker of the Pleiades alongside other celestial bodies; the retained correspondence concerns the explicitly shared Pleiades, not an identification of the other names.

The Lord asks whether Job can lead the Evening Star. Job's earlier speech had explicitly named God as its maker; this connection does not identify the accompanying untranslated mazourōth with any other celestial object.

The Lord asks about heaven's turnings and related happenings beneath heaven. Genesis assigns heavenly lights roles in signs, seasons, days and years upon earth, providing a particular creation account of celestial and terrestrial order.

The Lord asks whether a cloud will obey Job's voice with a violent trembling of water. Elihu had attributed numbered raindrops, rain and cloud covering to God; the later question probes Job's command of those same phenomena.

The Lord asks whether Job can send thunderbolts that answer him. The psalm attributes making lightning for rain to God, distinguishing divine provision of lightning from the human authority challenged in Job.

The Lord asks who gives women wisdom in weaving and embroidery. Exodus describes women wise in heart spinning materials for the sanctuary, a concrete instance of the textile skill named in the question.

The question attributes weaving and embroidery knowledge to its giver. Exodus explicitly attributes the craftsmen's wisdom and knowledge, including weaving and embroidery, to God's Spirit and His filling of their minds; the recipients differ.

The Lord asks who counts clouds wisely. Elihu's preceding conditional statement considers understanding a cloud's extensions and God's tent; both address understanding cloud formations, while the later passage expressly asks who possesses that wisdom.

The Lord asks whether Job can hunt food for lions. The psalm describes young lions seeking prey and food from God, identifying the provider behind the question; it does not identify Job's additional dragons as lion cubs.

The Lord describes the creatures in beds and wooded ambush places. The psalm describes lions gathering to lie in their enclosures at sunrise; the parallel concerns sheltered resting places, not identical motives or circumstances.
The question about food for young ravens crying to the Lord closely matches the psalm's declaration that He feeds the young ravens who call upon Him.

God's provision for ravens in Job corresponds to Jesus' instruction to consider ravens that God feeds. Luke applies the animal example to the disciples' anxiety about food; no direct quotation of Job is asserted.

The Lord assigns the wild donkey a wilderness and salt-marsh dwelling. The psalm describes God-provided mountain waters giving wild donkeys drink, another aspect of their provision beyond household domestication.

relationship: freedom from the tax collector's voice
rationale: The wild donkey does not hear a tax collector's reproach, while Job's earlier death-lament described the age-old ones not hearing a tax collector's voice. The specific auditory image is shared, with wilderness life and death remaining distinct settings.
The Lord describes the wild donkey seeking pasture and green growth. Job had asked whether a wild donkey cries without seeking food, using the same animal's feeding behavior for a different argument.

The Lord challenges the assumption that a one-horned beast will submit to human service. Balaam's oracle uses that creature's glory in describing deliverance from Egypt; the shared animal image does not establish a modern species identification.

The female creature leaves eggs upon the earth. Deuteronomy explicitly addresses birds' nests and eggs upon the ground, but gives a human command about taking them; it does not identify Job's untranslated creature names.

Job's creature neglects the danger of eggs being scattered or trampled. The Assyrian boast compares seizing the world to lifting abandoned eggs, using the vulnerability of unattended eggs for a distinct imperial image.

The creature treats its offspring as though not her own. Lamentations contrasts nursing creatures with the people's infants left thirsty and without bread; the link concerns failed care and does not equate Job's creature with its sparrow.

The Lord says He withheld understanding from this creature, having just asked who grants women textile wisdom. The comparison concerns His differing distribution of knowledge, without assigning the creature a modern zoological identity.
The Lord asks who clothed the horse with power. The psalm recognizes a horse's abundant power yet denies that it secures salvation, distinguishing created strength from dependable deliverance.
The Lord's question portrays the horse clothed with armor and daring. The proverb likewise speaks of a horse prepared for war, while locating help in the Lord rather than preparation itself.

The horse laughs at missiles and does not retreat from iron. The dragon's later portrait goes further by describing weapons as ineffective; this contrasts fearlessness with imperviousness rather than claiming the horse cannot be wounded.

The warhorse's expectation of the trumpet is followed by its reaction when the trumpet sounds: approval and recognition of war. The repeated signal joins anticipation and response within the same portrait.

The horse recognizes war when the trumpet sounds. Numbers prescribes a trumpet signal during battle against adversaries, supplying a distinct military use of the sound; it does not identify Job's horse with Israel's army.

The Lord asks whether the hawk's southward wing-spreading depends on Job's knowledge. Jeremiah contrasts birds knowing their appointed times with people not knowing divine judgments; the comparison does not equate the differently named birds or assert migration in Job.

The Lord's questions place a soaring eagle alongside a nesting vulture. Jeremiah compares an insolent high dwelling to an eagle's raised nest and promises to bring it down. The comparison concerns high birds and nests, while preserving Job's separate names for the soaring and nesting birds.
The high-nesting bird lodges on a rocky projection in a hidden place. Balaam describes the Kenite's strong dwelling through a nest set in rock, a figurative use of the secure nesting location.

The Lord describes the nesting vulture watching from afar for food. Job earlier compared his passing life with an eagle flying in search of food. This repeats bird-foraging imagery with different birds and purposes; the earlier lament stresses a vanishing trace.

Job's nesting birds are found wherever the dead are. Jesus' saying likewise joins a corpse with gathered birds, explicitly naming eagles. This is a shared corpse-and-birds image with different bird wording and discourse functions.

Job describes birds found where the dead lie. Jesus answers the question of where with the image of a body and gathered eagles; the connection is the explicit image, not a claim of identical narrative circumstances.

The Lord asks whether the one reproving Him will answer the judgment. Job had already pictured the difficulty of a mortal entering judgment with God and answering His words, anticipating the judicial problem now posed.
Job had expressed his wish to speak and argue before the Lord. The Lord's question now requires an answer from the one reproving God, bringing Job's desired encounter into the dialogue.

Job places a hand over his mouth when confronted by God's questions. Micah describes nations placing hands over their mouths and fearing the Lord after seeing His wonders; the shared gesture accompanies recognition of divine strength in different subjects.
Job now declines to add further words. Earlier he had offered to answer when God called or spoke; the contrast traces the change from readiness to reply to restraint after hearing the challenge.
The renewed divine reply from the cloud recalls the first address through whirlwind and clouds. Both notices identify the divine speaker and atmospheric setting of the two addresses.
God answers Job from a cloud. At Sinai the Lord announces that He will come in a pillar of cloud so the people can hear Him speaking to Moses, a corresponding mode of manifested divine speech.
The command to gird the waist and answer God's questions repeats the opening challenge of the first divine address. Its recurrence signals another examination of Job's presumed capacity.

The Lord states that His dealings are intended to show Job righteous. In the prologue He had already affirmed Job's innocence after undeserved loss, grounding this comparison in the edition's positive description of Job.

The Lord's stated purpose of showing Job righteous leads into His final vindication of Job against the friends. This follows the Saints wording and does not replace it with an accusation that Job condemns God to justify himself.

God describes a purpose of showing Job righteous. Peter likewise describes trials as demonstrating genuine faith; this compares the stated testing purpose without treating Job as the direct addressee of Peter's letter.
The Lord asks whether Job can thunder with a voice like His. The psalm calls thunder God's glorious, powerful voice, supplying the divine capability against which Job is measured.

The challenge tells Job to clothe himself with glory and honor. The psalm actually attributes greatness and clothing in praise and dignity to the Lord, illuminating the divine stature the challenge asks Job to assume.
The Lord challenges Job to humble every insolent person. Isaiah identifies a day belonging to the Lord against the insolent and elevated, when their height is humbled and He alone is exalted.

The challenge asks Job to make the ungodly decay immediately. The psalm anticipates the sinner's disappearance even when his place is sought, a judgment outcome the question challenges Job to accomplish.

The challenge describes hiding the wicked in the earth with dishonor. Isaiah tells people to hide in the earth from the Lord's terror and glorious strength; both connect earthly concealment with divine abasement, through different actions.

The Lord makes acknowledgment of Job's saving right hand conditional on the preceding feats. The psalm denies that the people's own arm saved them and credits God's right hand and arm, making the contrast in saving agency explicit.

The creature eats grass like oxen. The psalm attributes the sprouting of grass for livestock to God, supplying the provider for the dietary comparison without identifying this creature as a particular species.

The grass-eating creature's strength is located in loin and navel, while the later dragon portrait places power in its neck. The comparison concerns bodily power in distinct portraits, not identification of the creatures with each other.

The creature's ribs and spine are compared with bronze and iron. The later dragon description uses bronze shields for its inward parts; both employ metal imagery to convey formidable bodily structure.

The first portrait says the Lord formed the creature to be played with by His angels. The dragon portrait repeats that purpose; the shared wording does not establish that the two descriptions name the same creature.

This description names four-footed creatures in Tartarus rejoicing; the later dragon portrait treats the Tartarus of the abyss like a captive. The connection preserves their unusual shared terminology without explaining either as ordinary terrestrial habitat.

The first creature's snaring and nose-piercing question is followed by questions about hooking and binding the dragon's nose and lip. The sequence repeats capture imagery while preserving the distinction between the portraits.

The Lord asks whether Job can hook and muzzle a dragon. Ezekiel depicts Pharaoh as a river dragon whose jaws God will trap, contrasting a human's challenged ability with the action claimed by God in the oracle.

The dragon-capture question involves a nostril ring and pierced lip. The Assyrian oracle uses a muzzle in the nose and bridle in the lips for God's restraint of an arrogant ruler; it is a shared image, not shared personal identity.

The Lord's dragon question describes binding the nostril and lip. The parallel Assyrian oracle in Kings describes divine hooks in nostrils and a bridle in lips, applying physical restraint language to a ruler's forced return.

The Lord asks whether the dragon will covenant to become Job's permanent slave. Exodus describes a human slave voluntarily choosing permanent service; it supplies a legal counterpart to the servitude image without making the creature subject to that law.

Job is asked whether he can play with the dragon like a child's bird. The following portrait says it was made for angelic play, contrasting the proposed human handling with the purpose actually stated.

The question asks whether nations will feed on the dragon and clans divide it. The psalm depicts God crushing a dragon and giving it as food to Ethiopian peoples; the shared poetic image does not prove biological or historical identity.

The warning against laying a hand on the dragon invokes warfare within its body. The following portrait describes weapons accomplishing nothing against it; the link concerns dangerous confrontation and leaves the unusual internal-warfare wording unexplained.

After speaking of the creature prepared for Him, God asks who has stood against Him. Paul likewise raises resistance to God's purpose and challenges the human answering back, sharing the rhetorical challenge to presumed human opposition.

The Lord grounds His challenge in ownership of everything beneath heaven. His covenant speech at Sinai likewise declares that all the earth is His, even while distinguishing Israel as His treasured people.

Everything beneath heaven belongs to the divine speaker in Job. The psalm likewise assigns the earth, its fullness and its inhabitants to the Lord, directly matching the declaration of comprehensive ownership.

The dragon's inward parts are pictured as bronze shields. The preceding creature's ribs and spine are pictured as bronze and iron, a shared bodily-strength image that does not identify the two creatures as one.

The interlocking parts hold together and cannot be pulled apart; later the joined flesh cannot be shaken. These two descriptions repeat bodily cohesion within the same dragon portrait without replacing the wording with an anatomical species claim.

relationship: dawn imagery within the divine speech
rationale: The dragon's eyes resemble the dawn-bearer's appearance. Earlier the Lord named the dawn-bearer's appointed place when discussing morning brightness; this repeats dawn imagery without identifying the creature with a celestial being.

The dragon's mouth emits burning torches. The psalm describes fire from God's face setting things ablaze; both use emitted fire in a bodily portrayal, but the subjects and narrative functions remain different.
The dragon's nostril smoke is compared to a burning furnace. Abraham sees the destroyed plain's rising flame compared to furnace vapor, a shared furnace image with different sources and occasions.

The dragon's soul is described as coals and its mouth emits flame. The psalm likewise combines emitted fire and kindled coals in its portrayal of God; this is an imagery comparison, not an identification of God with the dragon.

Power lodges in the dragon's neck. The preceding grass-eating creature's description locates strength in loin and navel, presenting formidable bodily power in distinct creatures and different body regions.

The flesh is joined and unshaken. The earlier description of the dragon's interlocking inward parts similarly says they cling together without separation, repeating the body's resistant cohesion within the portrait.

The dragon's heart is fixed like stone and an anvil. Ezekiel uses a stone heart as an image of the human condition God replaces with a heart of flesh; the shared image serves different physical and moral purposes.

Four-footed beasts leap in fear when the dragon turns. In the preceding creature's portrait four-footed creatures in Tartarus rejoice, providing contrasting animal reactions while leaving that unusual location wording intact.

Lances and spears accomplish nothing against the dragon. The warhorse instead meets missiles without retreating from iron; the comparison distinguishes invulnerability in one portrait from courage in the other.

The dragon treats iron and bronze as straw and rotten wood. The earlier creature's ribs and spine are compared to bronze and iron, contrasting the uses of metal imagery within two depictions of formidable creatures.

The dragon regards a stone-thrower as grass, following its treatment of iron as straw and bronze as decayed wood. The repeated comparisons turn hard weapons into weak plant material within the same portrait.

The dragon laughs at a shaken fire-bearing weapon, as the warhorse laughs when meeting a missile. The repeated laughter image conveys defiance of weapons without implying the horse shares the dragon's stated invulnerability.

The sea's gold is like immeasurable mud beneath the dragon. Zechariah describes Tyre gathering gold like road mud; both compare gold with mud, with different subjects and rhetorical purposes rather than a shared event.

The dragon regards the abyss as a walking place. The Lord earlier asked whether Job had walked the abyss's tracks, creating a specific contrast between the creature's portrayed domain and the human experience being challenged.

The dragon treats the Tartarus of the abyss like a captive. The earlier creature's description also names Tartarus and four-footed creatures there; this preserves the shared unusual image without resolving its geography or identifying the creatures.
The dragon is said to be made for play by God's angels. The preceding creature's formation has the same stated purpose, a direct verbal correspondence between distinct portraits.

The dragon's making and angelic play in Job parallel the psalm's dragon formed by God for play. The play participants are phrased differently, so the connection is limited to the explicitly shared formation-and-play motif.

The dragon is called king of all things in the waters. Ezekiel identifies Pharaoh king of Egypt as a great dragon claiming ownership of his rivers, using comparable aquatic rule imagery without identifying him with Job's creature.

Job declares that God can do all things and nothing is impossible for Him. The promise concerning Sarah asks whether any word is impossible with God, expressing divine capability in a specific promised birth.

Job affirms God's unrestricted capability. Gabriel likewise declares that no word from God will be powerless in the announcement to Mary; the comparison preserves Luke's wording about God's word rather than substituting another translation.
Job repeats the Lord's question about hidden counsel and words before confessing his own lack of understanding. The shared wording directly links the final response to the opening divine challenge.

Job now admits not understanding great and wonderful things. Earlier he had already called God's works great, unsearchable and extraordinary; the response turns that assertion into an acknowledgment of his own limits.

Job echoes the language of questioning and answering but asks God to teach him. The Lord's earlier challenge had required Job to answer divine questions, so the reprise makes the changed roles explicit.

Job's final statement contrasts hearing of God with now seeing Him. Earlier he appealed to his own eye and ear concerning the matters under discussion; the recurring senses language has a different, explicitly divine object here.
Job regards himself as earth and ashes after the divine encounter. Abraham uses that same self-description while addressing the Lord, linking the bodily image with humility in divine-human speech.

God says Eliphaz and his two friends did not speak truth as Job did. Elihu's introduction had already criticized the three for declaring Job ungodly without answering him, a narrative counterpart that preserves the different speakers' assessments.

The Lord again calls Job His servant and distinguishes him from the friends. The prologue had already named him My servant Job and commended his truth and blamelessness, framing the book with divine approval.

God requires the friends to seek Job's offering and prayer to escape destruction. He likewise directs Abimelech to Abraham's prayer so he may live: a specific pattern of divinely appointed intercession under a threat of death. Genesis separately preserves Abimelech's pure-hearted ignorance and prevention from sin.

Job's friends must bring seven calves and seven rams. Balaam likewise asks Balak to prepare seven calves and seven rams; the exact animal-number correspondence does not equate the settings, intentions or religious evaluation of the offerings.

God promises to accept Job's prayer for the friends. James teaches praying for one another and attributes great strength to a righteous person's petition, offering a corresponding statement about effective intercession.

The friends obey and their sin is released through Job. The prologue described Job repeatedly offering sacrifices over his children's possible wrongdoing, establishing his earlier role in seeking cleansing on behalf of others.
